bmt-2021-discrete-tiebreaker-01.title: Mod 4
bmt-2021-discrete-tiebreaker-01.body:
Squares are $0$ or $1\pmod4$, so $n^2+1\equiv1$ or $2\pmod4$, never $0$. Since $4\mid2020$, no $n$ works.

**Answer: 0**

bmt-2021-discrete-tiebreaker-02.title: Simon's Favorite Factoring Trick
bmt-2021-discrete-tiebreaker-02.body:
$100$ gradians $=90^\circ$, so $1^\circ=\frac{10}9$ gradians. The interior angle of a regular $m$-gon is $\frac{180(m-2)}m$ degrees, which is $\frac{10}9\cdot\frac{180(m-2)}m$ gradians. Setting this equal to $\frac{180(n-2)}{n}$: $10n(m-2)=9m(n-2)$, i.e. $mn+18m-20n=0$, i.e. $(m-20)(n+18)=-360$.

So $20-m=d$ and $n+18=\frac{360}{d}$, with $d$ a divisor of $360$ and $n+18>18$, i.e. $d<20$, so there are $12$ such divisors (half of the $24$) giving $12$ positive solutions. One of them is $m=n=2$, which is not a polygon. So $11$ pairs: $(5,6),(8,12),(10,18),(11,22),(12,27),(14,42),(15,54),(16,72),(17,102),(18,162),(19,342)$.

**Answer: 11**

bmt-2021-discrete-tiebreaker-03.title: Parity, then the last term is forced
bmt-2021-discrete-tiebreaker-03.body:
The last $51$ entries are even, so the total is even exactly when the first $99$ sum to an even number, i.e. an even number of them are odd (from $\{3,5,7,11\}$, $4$ choices each; the only even choice is $2$). The number of such $99$-tuples is $\sum_i\binom{99}{2i}4^{2i}=\frac{5^{99}-3^{99}}2$.

Choose entries $100$ to $149$ freely ($4^{50}$ ways). Then the sum so far is even, and exactly one of $2,4,6,8$ makes the total divisible by $8$. So $N=\frac{5^{99}-3^{99}}2\cdot4^{50}=2^{99}(5^{99}-3^{99})=10^{99}-6^{99}$.

Modulo $1000$: $10^{99}\equiv0$, and $6^{99}\equiv0\pmod8$ and $6^{99}\equiv6^{-1}\equiv21\pmod{125}$ (since $6^{100}\equiv1$), so $6^{99}\equiv896\pmod{1000}$. Hence $N\equiv-896\equiv104$.

**Answer: 104**
